transcript.heading: News Report One (British Male)
paras: The government of Norway announced this week that it will completely ban the sale of new gasoline and diesel-powered cars by 2025, making it one of the first countries in the world to set such an ambitious deadline for transitioning to zero-emission vehicles. The policy, which was agreed upon by all major political parties, also includes significant tax incentives for electric vehicle purchases, including exemption from sales tax and reduced road tolls and parking fees. Norway already leads the world in electric vehicle adoption, with electric cars making up approximately 80 percent of new car sales in recent months, far higher than any other country. Government officials say the policy is essential for meeting the country's climate change targets, which include reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 55 percent from 1990 levels by 2030 and becoming carbon neutral by 2050. Critics have raised concerns about the availability of charging infrastructure, particularly in rural areas, though the government has pledged to invest heavily in expanding the charging network over the next three years. The policy applies only to new car sales; gasoline and diesel cars already on the road will be allowed to continue operating after 2025.
Questions 1 to 3 are based on the news report you have just heard. (British Female)

3. What concern have critics raised about the policy?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Female)
paras: A missing hiker from Portland, Oregon, was found safe and in good condition this morning after surviving five days lost in the Cascade Mountains with only minimal supplies. Twenty-two-year-old Maya Carter had been hiking alone when she wandered off the main trail during a sudden snowstorm last Saturday. Search and rescue teams had been searching the area since she was reported missing on Sunday, using helicopters, dogs, and ground crews. Carter told rescuers she had survived by taking shelter under fallen trees at night, melting snow for drinking water, and eating a small supply of granola bars and dried fruit she had brought with her. She said she had followed basic wilderness safety advice, staying in one place and making herself visible to search aircraft when she heard them overhead. Carter was transported to a local hospital for evaluation and was reported to be suffering only from mild dehydration and cold exposure. Park officials are reminding all hikers to check weather forecasts before heading out and to carry adequate supplies, even for short day hikes.
Questions 4 and 5 are based on the news report you have just heard. (British Female)
4. How many days was Maya Carter lost in the mountains?
5. What wilderness safety advice did Carter follow that helped her?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: The world's largest offshore wind farm officially began full operation this week off the coast of Yorkshire in the United Kingdom. The Hornsea One project, developed by a Danish energy company, consists of 174 wind turbines spread across an area of approximately 407 square kilometers in the North Sea. The farm has a total capacity of 1.2 gigawatts, enough to power over one million homes with clean, renewable electricity. Officials say the project represents a major milestone in the UK's efforts to reduce carbon emissions and meet its target of net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. The construction of the wind farm created more than 2,000 jobs during the building phase, and the project will continue to support hundreds of permanent positions in operations and maintenance. Each turbine stands 190 meters tall from sea level to the tip of the blade at its highest point, and the project includes a network of undersea cables that transmit electricity to the national grid. A second phase of the project, Hornsea Two, is already under construction nearby and is expected to be even larger when completed.
Questions 6 and 7 are based on the news report you have just heard. (British Female)

7. What is the total capacity of the Hornsea One wind farm?

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Travel Agent): Good afternoon, Welcome to Horizon Travel. How can I help you today?

Man (Customer): Hi there. I'm looking to book a flight from London to Bangkok for a vacation in late November. I need to be there by November 25th. Could you tell me what options are available and roughly how much they cost?

Woman: Sure! Let me check that for you. When are you hoping to return, and is there any flexibility with your dates? Sometimes flights can be significantly cheaper if you can leave a day earlier or later.

Man: I'm pretty flexible. I can leave anywhere between November 20th and 23rd, and I'd like to come back around December 15th. I'd prefer not to have really long layovers if possible—anything under three hours is fine, but I don't want to be stuck in an airport for eight hours somewhere.

Woman: Okay, let me look at the options. There are several airlines that fly that route. If you're willing to have one layover in Dubai, Emirates has flights for around 580 pounds return, and the layover is about two hours each way. Or you can fly direct with Thai Airways or British Airways, but direct flights are a bit more expensive—around 780 pounds return.
Man: Hmm, 780 is a bit more than I was hoping to spend. The Emirates option sounds good—two-hour layover in Dubai is totally fine. Is that for economy class?
Woman: Yes, that's economy. Would you like me to check prices leaving on November 22nd and returning December 14th? Those dates seem to have the best availability right now.
Man: That works perfectly for me. One more question—what's the baggage allowance? I usually check one suitcase and bring a carry-on.

Woman: Emirates allows 30 kilograms of checked baggage for economy class on that route, plus a carry-on bag up to 7 kilograms. That's pretty generous. Would you like to go ahead and book that, or would you like some time to think about it?
Man: Let's go ahead and book it, please. Can I pay with a credit card?
Woman: Absolutely. I'll just need your passport details and your card. And I'll email you the itinerary and e-ticket confirmation right away once the booking is complete.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard. (British Female)

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (American Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Lily): Hi James, how was your weekend? I heard you went to that new photography exhibit at the modern art museum.

Man (James): It was absolutely fantastic! I went with a couple of friends on Saturday afternoon. The photographer is a Japanese artist who specializes in landscape photography of remote areas in Iceland and northern Canada. The photos were huge—some of them were over two meters wide—and the colors were just stunning. You really felt like you were standing there in those landscapes.
Woman: That sounds amazing. I've been wanting to visit more art exhibits lately, but I feel like I never know what's good or what I should see. How did you hear about this one?

Man: I follow a few art blogs, and I also get a monthly newsletter from the museum that lists their upcoming exhibits. It's worth signing up for—they also send members discount offers and invitations to special opening nights. Are you a member of any museums?
Woman: No, I'm not. Is membership expensive? I go to museums maybe once every couple of months, so I'm not sure if it would be worth it.

Man: A basic membership at the modern art museum is only 35 pounds a year, and that gives you free entry to all their exhibits, plus discounts at the gift shop and cafe. Since regular tickets are about 12 pounds each, you only need to go three times a year for it to pay for itself. They also have evening events and lectures that are free for members.

Woman: That actually sounds pretty reasonable. Did you know they're having a special lecture next month by a well-known wildlife photographer? I saw a poster for it on campus. I wonder if members get priority booking for that.

Man: I think they do! Members usually get to book tickets for special events a week before they go on sale to the general public. Let me check the museum website when I get home and send you the link to sign up. If we're both members, we could go to exhibits together more often.
Woman: That sounds great. I'd really like that. I've also been meaning to check out the portrait gallery downtown—have you been there before?

Man: Yes, I went a few months ago. They have a wonderful permanent collection, and they also have temporary exhibits. It's actually free to enter the permanent collection; you only pay for the special exhibits. But that's another place where a membership would come in handy if you go regularly.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Male)
paras: The world's first modern suspension bridge, the Brooklyn Bridge in New York City, was an engineering marvel when it opened to the public on May 24, 1883, connecting the boroughs of Manhattan and Brooklyn across the East River. Designed by German-American engineer John Augustus Roebling, the bridge was the longest suspension bridge in the world at the time of its completion, with a main span of 486 meters. Roebling, who had previously designed several smaller suspension bridges, conceived the project after years of frustration with unreliable ferry service across the river. Unfortunately, Roebling never lived to see his bridge completed; he died of tetanus in 1869 after an accident while surveying the site, and the project was completed by his son Washington Roebling, who himself suffered from decompression sickness after working in the underwater caissons used to build the bridge's foundations. Washington Roebling was left partially paralyzed by the condition and supervised much of the remaining construction from his apartment overlooking the site, with his wife Emily Warren Roebling relaying his instructions to workers and learning advanced engineering principles to help manage the project. At the time of opening, many people were skeptical that the bridge was structurally sound, so the city arranged for a parade of 21 elephants to cross the bridge in 1884 to demonstrate its stability. Today, the Brooklyn Bridge carries approximately 100,000 vehicles and 10,000 pedestrians across the East River every day and remains one of the most iconic landmarks in New York City, designated a National Historic Landmark in 1964.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Female)
paras: Learning to play a musical instrument is a rewarding activity that offers numerous cognitive, emotional, and social benefits at any age, and contrary to a common misconception, it is never too late to start. Many adults avoid learning an instrument because they believe the myth that you must start as a child to become proficient, but research consistently shows that adults can achieve high levels of musical ability with consistent practice. Learning an instrument engages multiple areas of the brain simultaneously, improving memory, attention span, spatial reasoning, and even language skills. Studies have found that children who study music tend to perform better in mathematics and reading, but older adults also benefit: research has shown that learning an instrument later in life can help delay cognitive decline and reduce the risk of dementia. Playing music also serves as an excellent stress reliever, lowering cortisol levels and providing a creative outlet for self-expression. Choosing which instrument to learn is a personal decision based on your musical preferences, physical considerations, and budget. The piano is often recommended for beginners because it provides a straightforward introduction to musical theory, with notes laid out in a logical pattern, while the guitar is highly portable and versatile for many musical styles. Regardless of which instrument you choose, experts recommend starting with a qualified teacher to develop good technique from the beginning, practicing consistently for short daily sessions rather than occasional long sessions, and choosing music you enjoy playing to maintain motivation. Many communities have amateur music groups and community bands that welcome adult beginners, providing a social environment and performance opportunities as you progress.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: The history of chocolate spans more than 3,000 years, beginning with the ancient civilizations of Mesoamerica in present-day Mexico and Central America. The Olmec, Maya, and Aztec peoples all cultivated the cacao tree and prepared cacao beans as a bitter, frothy beverage, often flavored with chili peppers, vanilla, and honey. Unlike the sweet chocolate we know today, this drink was considered a luxury and was used in religious ceremonies and even as a form of currency among the Aztecs, who believed cacao was a gift from the god Quetzalcoatl. Chocolate was introduced to Europe in the 16th century after the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire, where it was initially served as a drink sweetened with sugar or honey, popular among the Spanish nobility. Over the next several centuries, chocolate spread throughout Europe, with chocolate houses becoming popular gathering places in cities like London and Paris in the 17th and 18th centuries. The Industrial Revolution brought major changes to chocolate production: in 1828, a Dutch chemist named Coenraad van Houten invented a process to make cocoa powder, which made chocolate cheaper and more consistent. In 1847, the first solid eating chocolate was developed in Britain by Fry and Sons, and in 1875, Swiss chocolatier Daniel Peter invented milk chocolate by adding powdered milk to the chocolate mixture. These innovations transformed chocolate from an expensive luxury beverage into an affordable, widely available food. Today, chocolate is produced and consumed around the world, with major producing countries including Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, and Indonesia, though concerns about fair labor practices and environmental sustainability in cacao farming have led to increased demand for fair-trade and ethically produced chocolate.
